\chapter{And, Or, But}
\label{ch:ka-and-or-but}
\hlchaptermodality{67}

\begin{chapteropening}
\textbf{By the end of this chapter:} \emph{I can join two Kannada ideas with and, or and but, and I can add myself to what somebody else said.}

Complete KA-C67-and-too and join two things four different ways.
\end{chapteropening}

\section[mattu]{\kn{ಮತ್ತು} (mattu) — and}

\label{lesson:KA-C67-and}



\begin{quote}
Before the new one: what did \emph{beḷe} mean? And \emph{suggi}?
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: \kn{ಮತ್ತು}}
\textbf{\kn{ಮತ್ತು}} (\emph{mattu}) — \textquotedblleft{}and\textquotedblright{}.

It stands between the two things it joins, in the same place English puts \emph{and}: \textbf{\kn{ಚಹಾ} \kn{ಮತ್ತು} \kn{ಕಾಫಿ}} (\emph{cahā mattu kāphi}) — \textquotedblleft{}tea and coffee\textquotedblright{}.

You have had a hundred and thirty nouns and no way to say two of them in one breath. Every list so far had to be a series of separate sentences. This is the word that ends that.

A note on how it is actually said. In unhurried speech Kannada will often join two nouns by simply naming them one after the other, with nothing between; \kn{ಮತ್ತು} is what a careful sentence, a notice or a written list reaches for. Both are ordinary standard-colloquial Kannada, and \kn{ಮತ್ತು} is the one that never sounds wrong.

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
The first join. Two things, one sentence.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Say it:} \emph{mattu}
  \item \emph{Say it:} \emph{cahā mattu kāphi}
  \item \emph{Say it:} join two words you already know with \emph{mattu}
  \item \emph{Recall:} say \emph{beḷe}, then say \emph{suggi}
  \item \emph{Recall:} from much earlier — say \emph{kṛtajñate}, \emph{bīḷkoḍuge}, \emph{horaḍu}, \emph{prayāṇa}, and say what each one means
  \item \emph{Recall:} say \emph{vinanti}, then read \textbf{\kn{ಅನುಮತಿ}}
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What does \kn{ಮತ್ತು} mean? (\textquotedblleft{}and\textquotedblright{}.) Name two things you own, joined with it.
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[ma]{\kn{ಮ} — one character, met inside words you already say}

\label{lesson:KA-S134-letter-ma}



\begin{quote}
Before the new one: \kn{ಞ} — where would you nearly always meet it?

One character this time. Just one — and this is the one you have been reading longest without being told. It sits in more of the words in this book than any other character nobody has named.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{Script you'll notice: \kn{ಮ}}
\textbf{\kn{ಮ}} — \emph{ma}.

It is a \textbf{consonant}, and in this script a consonant is never bare: it comes with an \emph{a} already in it. So it is not \emph{m}, it is \textbf{ma}.

You already say these, and every one of them has \kn{ಮ} somewhere inside it:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textbf{\kn{ಮತ್ತು}} \emph{mattu} — and, from the lesson before this one
  \item \textbf{\kn{ಮರ}} \emph{mara} — a tree
  \item \textbf{\kn{ಮೋಡ}} \emph{mōḍa} — a cloud
  \item \textbf{\kn{ನಮಸ್ಕಾರ}} \emph{namaskāra} — the greeting you opened this book with
\end{itemize}

\subsection*{Writing: \kn{ಮ}}
Put your pen on \kn{ಮ} and follow its line. Copy the shape you can see — slowly, and larger than it is printed.

\begin{quote}
This book does not yet tell you \textbf{where to start the character or which way to travel}. That is a real thing, taught with real variation from school to school, and it is not written down here until it can be written down with a source. Copying what is in front of you needs no such source, and it is how the shape gets into your hand in the meantime.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{Your turn}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Look:} at these words, and find \kn{ಮ} in the ones that have it
\end{itemize}

\begin{quote}
\kn{ಮತ್ತು}  ·  \kn{ಮರ}  ·  \kn{ನಮಸ್ಕಾರ}
\end{quote}

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Trace it:} \kn{ಮ} three times, saying \emph{ma} as you finish each one
  \item \emph{Look:} back at any page of this chapter and find \kn{ಮ} once more
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Which character is this — \kn{ಮ}? What sound does it carry? (\emph{\textbf{ma}}.) Name one word you already say that contains it.
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[athavā]{\kn{ಅಥವಾ} (athavā) — or}

\label{lesson:KA-C67-or}



\begin{quote}
Before the new one: what did \emph{mattu} do between two words? And which character did you meet inside it?
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: \kn{ಅಥವಾ}}
\textbf{\kn{ಅಥವಾ}} (\emph{athavā}) — \textquotedblleft{}or\textquotedblright{}.

It goes where \kn{ಮತ್ತು} went, between the two things — but now the two are alternatives instead of a pair: \textbf{\kn{ಚಹಾ} \kn{ಅಥವಾ} \kn{ಕಾಫಿ}?} (\emph{cahā athavā kāphi?}) — \textquotedblleft{}tea or coffee?\textquotedblright{}

That one question is most of what a host says and most of what a shop asks, and until this word there was no way to put a choice to anybody.

\kn{ಅಥವಾ} is a Sanskrit word taken over whole — \emph{atha} (\textquotedblleft{}then\textquotedblright{}) plus \emph{vā} (\textquotedblleft{}or\textquotedblright{}) — and it is at home in speech as well as on the page. Quick speech will also just name the two options with a rise between them, or slip \kn{ಇಲ್ಲ} in the gap; \kn{ಅಥವಾ} is the one that makes the choice unmistakable.

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
A pair, and now a choice.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Say it:} \emph{athavā}
  \item \emph{Say it:} \emph{cahā athavā kāphi?}
  \item \emph{Say it:} \emph{cahā mattu kāphi}, then \emph{cahā athavā kāphi} — and say which one is an offer of both
  \item \emph{Recall:} say \emph{mattu}, then name the character you traced last
  \item \emph{Recall:} from much earlier — say \emph{gaurava}, \emph{upakāra}, \emph{bahuśaḥ}, \emph{khaṇḍita}, and say what each one means
  \item \emph{Recall:} read \textbf{\kn{ಸಂಕೋಚ}}
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What does \kn{ಅಥವಾ} mean? (\textquotedblleft{}or\textquotedblright{}.) Offer somebody a choice between two drinks.
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[ādare]{\kn{ಆದರೆ} (ādare) — but}

\label{lesson:KA-C67-but}



\begin{quote}
Before the new one: which of \emph{mattu} and \emph{athavā} offers a choice?
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: \kn{ಆದರೆ}}
\textbf{\kn{ಆದರೆ}} (\emph{ādare}) — \textquotedblleft{}but\textquotedblright{}.

You have read it before without being told. The word for \textquotedblleft{}in that case\textquotedblright{} — \textbf{\kn{ಹಾಗಾದರೆ}} (\emph{hāgādare}) — is \kn{ಹಾಗೆ} (\emph{hāge}, \textquotedblleft{}that way\textquotedblright{}) with \kn{ಆದರೆ} welded on behind it. The piece you could not name was doing this job all along.

\textbf{\kn{ಚಹಾ} \kn{ಇದೆ}, \kn{ಆದರೆ} \kn{ಕಾಫಿ} \kn{ಇಲ್ಲ}} (\emph{cahā ide, ādare kāphi illa}) — \textquotedblleft{}there is tea, but there is no coffee.\textquotedblright{}

\kn{ಆದರೆ} opens the second half of the sentence, not the first, exactly as English \emph{but} does.

\begin{grammarlens}[title={Grammar Lens: a verb doing a conjunction's job}]
\kn{ಆದರೆ} is not a conjunction by birth. It is the verb \kn{ಆಗು} (\emph{āgu}, \textquotedblleft{}to become\textquotedblright{}) carrying the ending \textbf{-\kn{ದರೆ}} (\emph{-dare}), which is Kannada's \textquotedblleft{}if\textquotedblright{}. Read literally it says \textquotedblleft{}if it becomes\textquotedblright{} — \textquotedblleft{}granted that, all the same\textquotedblright{}.

That is why \kn{ಹಾಗಾದರೆ} means \textquotedblleft{}in that case\textquotedblright{}: \kn{ಹಾಗೆ} (\textquotedblleft{}that way\textquotedblright{}) \textbf{if it be}. One ending, two everyday words, and both of them turn out to be small sentences.
\end{grammarlens}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
Three joins now: and, or, but.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Say it:} \emph{ādare}
  \item \emph{Say it:} \emph{cahā ide, ādare kāphi illa}
  \item \emph{Say it:} \emph{hāgādare}, then take it apart into \emph{hāge} and \emph{ādare}
  \item \emph{Recall:} say \emph{athavā}, then offer a choice with it
  \item \emph{Recall:} from much earlier — say \emph{āśīrvāda}, \emph{sāku}, \emph{atithi}, \emph{raita}, and say what each one means
  \item \emph{Recall:} say \emph{nambike}
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What does \kn{ಆದರೆ} mean? (\textquotedblleft{}but\textquotedblright{}.) Which everyday word already had it inside? (\emph{hāgādare}.)
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[nānū]{\kn{ನಾನೂ} (nānū) — I too}

\label{lesson:KA-C67-and-too}



\begin{quote}
Before the new one: what did \emph{ādare} mean, and which verb is hiding inside it?
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: \kn{ನಾನೂ}}
\textbf{\kn{ನಾನೂ}} (\emph{nānū}) — \textquotedblleft{}I too, me as well\textquotedblright{}.

Look at what changed. \kn{ನಾನು} (\emph{nānu}, \textquotedblleft{}I\textquotedblright{}) became \kn{ನಾನೂ}: the last vowel got longer, and nothing else moved. That lengthening is a word in its own right — a suffix, \textbf{-\kn{ೂ}} (\emph{-ū}) — and it means \textquotedblleft{}as well\textquotedblright{}.

You already met \kn{ಕೂಡ} (\emph{kūḍa}) doing the same adding job as a separate word. \kn{ನಾನು} \kn{ಕೂಡ} and \kn{ನಾನೂ} say the same thing; the second one welds it on.

\begin{grammarlens}[title={Grammar Lens: the same ending on two nouns means both}]
Put \textbf{-\kn{ೂ}} on two nouns instead of one and you have said \textquotedblleft{}both\textquotedblright{}:

\textbf{\kn{ಹಾಲೂ} \kn{ನೀರೂ}} (\emph{hālū nīrū}) — \textquotedblleft{}both milk and water\textquotedblright{}.

So Kannada has two ways to join two nouns, and this lesson and the \kn{ಮತ್ತು} lesson have now given you each of them: a word that stands between, and an ending that rides on both. The second is the older Dravidian habit, and it is the one you will hear more often at a table.
\end{grammarlens}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
Four ways to put two ideas side by side: \kn{ಮತ್ತು}, \kn{ಅಥವಾ}, \kn{ಆದರೆ}, and now the ending \textbf{-\kn{ೂ}}.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Say it:} \emph{nānu}, then \emph{nānū}, and say which one adds you to somebody else
  \item \emph{Say it:} \emph{hālū nīrū}
  \item \emph{Say it:} all four joins in a row — \emph{mattu}, \emph{athavā}, \emph{ādare}, and \emph{-ū} on a noun
  \item \emph{Recall:} say \emph{kūḍa}, then say \emph{nānū}, and say what the two have in common
  \item \emph{Recall:} from much earlier — say \emph{vandane}, \emph{vaidya}, \emph{vidyārthi}, \emph{śikṣaka}, and say what each one means
  \item \emph{Recall:} read \textbf{\kn{ಸೌಜನ್ಯ}}, then say \emph{hola}
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What does \kn{ನಾನೂ} mean? (\textquotedblleft{}I too\textquotedblright{}.) Put the same ending on \kn{ಹಾಲು} and on \kn{ನೀರು} and say \textquotedblleft{}both\textquotedblright{}.
\end{tcolorbox}
